newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish securities law to set international norms.
newsitem.headline: Polish securities law to set international norms.

text.p: The Polish parliament is discussing a bill on trading which analysts say will help adjust the securities law to the norms of the European Union and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
The lower house, which started work on the bill late on Wednesday, sent it to parliamentary committees and final passage is expected in this year's second quarter.

Analysts said the law would create a legal framework for the introduction of new instruments such as futures and options and help Polish brokerages develop by granting them the right to provide investment-bank-type services.

"Brokerages' rights are too low...and there will be pressure for them to transform into investment banks, which is important because such banks which are formed in Poland know the local economic reality better than Western banks with decades of experience," said Waldemar Gebus of Raiffeisen Capital & Investment.

Analysts said foreign investors had sometimes been surprised to call a Polish broker to be told he or she was unauthorised to provide advice, while in coming months the same houses could start advising on public offerings and similar operations.
Another advantage was that only banks, brokerages and insurance firms would be allowed to underwrite issues, unlike current legislation, which allows any firm or even an individual to do so.

Analysts said that in addition to derivatives trade, which the bourse says could start in the second quarter, the law would permit investors to sell short -- selling instruments which are not owned in the hope of buying them back more cheaply later.
They said the law would also reduce some of the bureaucracy that has sometimes made the Polish market seem over-regulated.

Polish Securities Commission (KPW) head Jacek Socha has said that the bill would allow Polish companies to float up to 25 percent of shares abroad without the Securities Commission's permission, either directly or through depositary receipts.
After the year 2000, firms would be allowed to float an unlimited amount of stock abroad without a permit.

Socha, whose organisation drafted the bulk of the bill, has said companies whose shares were traded publicly for more than 36 months would no longer have to submit issue prospectuses for new share issues for Securities Commission approval, thereby simplifying the raising of capital.

The bill would let foreign brokerages open branches in Poland rather than having to register separate firms and allow for the creation of closed end investment funds. It would also give Polish citizens the opportunity to buy shares on international markets.
In addition, analysts welcomed the fact that the bill sought to provide recognition of beneficial ownership rights.
Some foreigners have complained that a broker cannot buy stock for a client and then transfer it to him. Instead, investors such as fund managers need to set up mirror accounts.

"(The law) should regulate so-called beneficial owner and legal owner cases. It contains specific regulations allowing for the facilitation of the functioning of foreign entities on the Polish capital market," Socha wrote on Thursday in the financial daily Nowa Europa.

The bill is also expected to encourage the privatisation of the Warsaw stock exchange, which has so far acted as a non-profit organisation largely controlled by the state treasury, by allowing bourse member securities houses to earmark up to 20 percent of profit for dividends.
